reasons: āśú- = ὠκύς and áśva- = ἵππος are exact cognates. RV 10.107.10a really has áśvam, āśúm in agreement, of a racehorse groomed for the patron. Homer has ὠκύς, ἵππος in 35 lines (Il. 10.474, 10.527, 11.127 checked; the expected count by chance is about 2), and the RV has 9 stanzas with both against about 1.7 expected (RV 1.117.9, 7.71.5, 10.78.5 checked). Both use the adjective of chariot and race horses. Avestan names with āsu-, aspa- add a third branch. The Greek anchor Il. 14.407 is a misfit: ὠκύ goes with βέλος. RV 10.68.2d has āśū́n used as a noun with no horse word. So the case rests on the RV 10.107 anchor and the support. Swift horses is a natural phrase, but the frequency and fixed epithet status on both sides go well beyond chance.

dyaùḥ = Ζεῦ (*dyēw-) and pítar = πάτερ (*ph₂ter) are exact. RV 6.51.5a is a true vocative pair with the second word unaccented, inside a prayer for mercy. Il. 19.121 is Hera's address to Zeus opening with Ζεῦ, πάτερ. Same speech act, same word order, same vocative syntax. Latin Iuppiter univerbates the same vocative. Not generic: a specific theonym, kin term, attested in three branches. RV 1.89.4b is the nominative variant inside the Sky-Earth merism. Homer has Ζεύς, πατήρ in 79 lines against about 10 expected.

The cognates are right: áhi- = aži- and vŕ̥ka- = vəhrka-. Anchors checked: RV 7.38.7c has áhim and vŕ̥kam, with the demons, as objects of jambháyantaḥ. AVŚ 4.3.7 lists stenam, ahim, yātudhānam and vṛkam. YtArW 2.8 has ažiciϑra and vəhrkō.ciϑra in a litany with the verb duuarata (preverb apa), and 2.11/2.15 have them with jaiṇti/janāt̰. All three are apotropaic catalogues that mix noxious animals with human or demonic evildoers, so the frame is congruent. But snake and wolf are the obvious pests of any herding people. Each Vedic text pairs them only once (RV 1 stanza, AV 1 sentence), the verbs differ, and the Avestan compounds with -ciϑra- are a different construction. Shared Indo-Iranian at most; possibly independent.

Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος is an exact neuter s-stem (*wékʷos). √śru- = κλύω (*ḱlew-). Both have a 1sg possessor. Homer has it exactly: Il. 16.236 has ἔπος as object of ἔκλυες, with the possessive ἐμόν, in Achilles' prayer to Zeus (verified), and Il. 14.234 has the same. The RV has the prayer formula of śr̥ṇavat with vácāṃsi and enclitic me in RV 10.66.11c, 1.145.3 and 10.65.13, all invoking gods to hear the poet. 8 RV stanzas have śru-, vácas- against about 3 expected. Same construction, same speech act, high-register 'word' on both sides. The Pindar anchor (I. 6.42) has ἔπος, ἐμάν next to Ζεῦ, πάτερ, but its verb is renewed (ἄκουσας) and it echoes Homer. RV 10.64.10b splits the verb (śr̥ṇotu) and the object vácaḥ across pādas. The Homeric support carries the claim.

The roots are cognate (him-/himá- ~ χειμών; ghr̥ṇá-/gharmá- ~ θέρος from *gʷʰer-), but the heat word is a different formation on each side. The anchors do not share a collocation. RV 10.37.10b is a blessing over light, cold and heat (himā́ beside ghr̥ṇéna, each with śám) in a list of conditions. Xenophon Cyr. 5.1.11 and Arist. GA 767a are prose about the seasons. The RV support (RV 1.119.6b, 8.73.3b, 1.116.8a: hiména, gharmám) is the Atri myth, where heat is quenched with cold, not a totality merism. A cold/heat or winter/summer polar pair built from each language's ordinary words is exactly the generic figure that arises independently. Same verdict as B143.

The Latin anchor CatAgr 141.3 checks out: pastores and pecua kept salua by seruassis in Cato's lustration prayer to Mars. The Iguvine prayer in Buck's text has ueiro, pequo ... salua, seritu (the VIa 30-32 type, repeated several times). So Lat. pecu = Umbr. pequo and saluus, seruare = salua, seritu are exact cognate pairs in identical prayer contexts. Latin renews *wiHro- as pastores. The 'men, livestock' merism links outward through Av. pasu, vīra (Y 9.4e, VS 10.18c, YtMihr 29.2h; 12 CAB units). This is a sound inherited formula. Caveat: the Vedic anchor RV 1.121.4a is irrelevant (the merism is in 3d, with dvipád/cátuṣpad, different words and not a petition). RV 1.114.1c is the real Vedic analogue but is a lexical renewal. The core Latin-Umbrian agreement is Italic-internal.

amṛ́ta- = ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥-tó-) and áśva- = ἵππος are exact. AVŚ 13.1.47 does have aśvāḥ ... amṛtāḥ (nom. pl.) drawing the Sun's chariot. Homer has ἄμβροτοι, ἵπποι for Achilles' god-given team (Il. 16.381 and 16.867, checked). The Plato anchor (Phaedrus 247e) is misdescribed as a witness: there the horses are fed ἀμβροσίαν; it is not the epithet. There is a single Vedic witness (RV: 5 stanzas with amŕ̥ta-, áśva-, at chance level, none attributive). 'Immortal' is a cheap epithet for anything belonging to gods, so independent formation is likely.

Same inherited formula as B113. AVŚ 3.23.14 and 9.10.23 have dyauḥ, pitā beside pṛthivī, mātā (9.10.23 = RV 1.164.33), and Cato Agr. 132.2 has the univerbated vocative Iupiter in a sacrificial address. Fully regular cognates in three branches, and the RV vocative (RV 6.51.5a) matches Ζεῦ, πάτερ. Caveats: the Aristotle anchor (Pol. 1259b) only quotes Homer's 'father of men and gods' for Zeus. It is derivative and not the appositional formula itself. In Latin, Iuppiter is a fused name, not a free phrase. The grade rests on the Vedic and Homeric material.

Lat. sus = ὗς and ouis = ὄις are exact; taurus = ταῦρος is a cognate or shared old word. The Xenophon anchor (Hell. 6.4.29) is a prose requisition of βοῦς, οἶς, αἶγας and ὗς for the Pythia: four animals, with βοῦς not ταῦρος. That is just a list of domestic livestock and only loosely congruent. Cato Agr. 141.3 has suouitaurilibus. The better Greek parallel, Od. 11.131 (ram, bull and boar to Poseidon: ταῦρον and συῶν with renewed ἀρνειόν), keeps two cognate members (ταῦρος, σῦς) and renews the sheep. A grouped offering of the three main domestic animals is natural in any pastoral cult, so the agreement may be cultural rather than phraseological. Defensible, not compelling.

nā́bhi- ~ ὀμφαλός (*h₃nobʰ-) is accepted, though the Greek -αλ- formation differs. The Vedic anchor RV 6.47.28b is 'navel of Varuṇa' (váruṇasya, nā́bhiḥ), said of the chariot, so it is not the earth formula. The cited RV 3.4.4c is the navel of heaven (diváḥ, nā́bhā), not earth. Genuine Vedic nā́bhā, pr̥thivyā́ḥ exists (RV 10.1.6b, 3.29.4b, 9.82.3b; 17 stanzas against about 2 expected). Greek has γᾶς, ὀμφαλός, and Ion 5-6 has ὀμφαλόν with μέσον, καθίζων. But the earth word is not cognate, and the navel-of-the-world image is cross-cultural. The *sed- seating verb on both sides is a nice touch but loosely matched.

rájas- = ἔρεβος (*h₁régʷos) is a sound equation. But no Vedic collocation with 'night' exists. In RV 1.116.20b, náktam is an adverb ('by night') and rájobhiḥ means 'through the spaces'; these are separate constituents, and only 2 RV stanzas have rájas-, nákt- (about 0.7 expected). RV 1.35.4d (kr̥ṣṇā́, rájāṃsi) has no night word. Greek ἐρεβεννός, νύξ (Il. 13.425) and Ἔρεβος beside Νύξ (Theog. 123) are Greek-internal: a derived adjective, and a genealogy. The 'drift' explanation (rájas lost 'dark' and needs kr̥ṣṇá-) is special pleading, and the colour adjectives are not cognate. Darkness associated with night is also generic.

nau- = ναῦς is exact. aritra- and -ορος/ἐρετμός share *h₁erh₁- 'row' but are different formations. AVŚ 17.1.116 (nāvam with śata- aritrām as epithet) and AVŚ 7.6.6 (su-, aritrām) are real numeral/su-, oar bahuvrīhis for a ship, and Homer has νηὸς, ἐεικοσόροιο (Od. 9.322). The Greek anchor Eur. Hel. 1267 has only ναῦν and separately ἐρετμῶν, not the compound, so it does not witness the claim. The numerals differ (hundred vs twenty/fifty). Describing ships by their number of oars is a technical habit any seafaring culture could arrive at. Defensible pattern-level parallel only.

The etymologies are good. jāgṛ-/jāgrat- = Av. jaγāurvah- = Gk ἐγρήγορα share the same reduplicated stem *h₁ge-h₁gor-, and svap- = ὕπνος (*swep-). The Vedic anchors (RV 10.164.3b, AVŚ 6.45.3, 6.96.3, 6.115.3, 7.108.3, 8.6.15) all really have the coordinated 'waking or sleeping' pair. The Indo-Iranian epithet pair ('sleepless, wakeful'; Av. jaγāurum in Y 62.5, YtZam 8.10) is a good Indo-Iranian match. But the Greek anchors (Ti. 52b ἄυπνον, Ti. 45d ὕπνος beside ἐγερθεῖσιν) are not a coordinated pair: different referents and a different verb (ἐγείρω simplex). The real Greek pair (Symp. 203a ἐγρηγορόσι, καθεύδουσι) renews the sleep member. 'Waking or sleeping' as a totality merism is universal and uses default words. The shared marked perfect stem lifts this above reject, but it is not compelling.

The Empedocles quotation in Arist. Metaph. 1000a (ἦν, ἔσθ’, ἔσται with repeated τε) and Avestan Y 33.10 (ā̊ŋharə̄, həṇtī, bauuaiṇtī) are real and checked. But the only shared lexeme is the default copula *h₁es-, and the formations differ (Greek imperfect vs Avestan perfect). The future slot is renewed in Indo-Iranian. Polysyndeton with *-kʷe is the ordinary way to coordinate in these languages. 'All that was, is and will be' is a universal totality formula (Semitic, Egyptian), built in each language from its ordinary verb 'be'. The Vedic anchor AVŚ 6.115.3-4 (bhūtaṃ, bhavyaṃ, past and future as things that free from sin) is not the tripartite relative-clause frame. Generic.

The cognates are correct: *swéh₂du- = svādú- = ἡδύς = swēte; *médʰu = mádhu = μέθυ = medu. The NP is real in three branches: μέθυ, ἡδύ is a Homeric line-end formula (9 lines, Od. 17.533 checked; the Telegonia line too); RV 1.84.10a has svādóḥ, mádhvaḥ (genitive NP); Finnsburg 39 has swētne, medo (checked in the OE text). In the Vedic anchor AVP 5.28.8, svādu and madhu are separate predicates of annam, not an NP. The Greek keeping the epithet after μέθυ drifted to 'wine' is a point in favour. But honey and mead are sweet by nature, so 'sweet, honey/mead' is the expected collocation in any language. Greek uses ἡδύς freely with οἶνος too. Shared vocabulary plausibly co-occurring anyway.

urú- = εὐρύς and pánthā- = πόντος (*pont-eh₁-) are both accepted. All anchors check: RV 3.54.9d, 4.26.5b, 8.68.13b and 10.107.1d have urú-, pánthā- in agreement; Il. 6.291, Il. 9.72, Od. 1.197 and Soph. Trach. 113 have εὐρύς, πόντος. RV 10 stanzas (about 2.3 expected); Homer 9 lines (about 0.8 expected). But εὐρύς is the generic Greek epithet of every expanse: with sea, earth, sky, gulf or back it has 51 Homeric lines. 'Wide road' is likewise a natural Vedic phrase. The semantic drift means the Greek phrase is 'wide sea', so the claimed preserved 'way' sense is an inference. A defensible double cognation, but explicable by generic epithet use. Same verdict as B146.

Only the noun is cognate: pati- = πόσις. The verbs differ (vid- vs εὑρίσκω, which is not from *weyd-), so the verb is unrelated vocabulary, not a renewal of a fixed formula. AVŚ 2.36.4 has pati, vedanam (a compound name for the charm, not the clause). AVŚ 14.2.45 (kanyā as subject of vindate with patim) and Od. 6.282 (πόσιν, εὗρεν) are real. 'Find a husband' is ordinary idiom in many languages, and Greek has it only in this scene. Coincidence of one common noun in a natural phrase.

Ved. ahann, ahim (AVŚ 2.5.11 = RV 1.32.2) and Av. janat̰, ažīm (Y 9.8a, 9.11a, checked) are exact cognates on both elements (*gʷʰen-, *h₁ógʷʰi-), in the same mythic act: a hero slays the serpent. Pindar P. 4.249 has κτεῖνε ... ὄφιν (Jason slays the guardian serpent). ὄφις is the exact cognate of the object, and the verb is renewed with κτείνω, a renewal of a well-known kind. The RV pair is formulaic (30 stanzas with áhi-, han- against about 2.7 expected). This meets the threshold: an exact Indo-Iranian pair plus the Greek object cognate in the same clause shape and context.

mel = μέλι and dulcis = γλυκύς are cognate. But the Greek anchors are misfits: Meteor. 4.10 and 4.8 only list μέλι beside the words γλυκύς, οἶνος and γλεῦκος in a chemistry list, which is no figure. Vedic renews both words (svā́dīyaḥ, mádhunaḥ, RV 8.24.20c), so only Latin and Greek share the wording. Plautus (Asin. 614) adapts Greek New Comedy, so the Latin lover's address could be derivative. 'Sweeter than honey' is a cross-cultural comparison (Semitic, Egyptian) built from default words. Homeric γλυκίων, μέλιτος (Il. 1.249, 18.109) is real but proves nothing beyond Greek.

δεξιός = dexter and λαιός = laeuus are cognate. The anchors check (Eur. Hel. 1573, Rhes. 485, IA 290; Lucr. 2.488, 4.301, 4.430). But coordinating 'right' and 'left' is inevitable once the words exist. The contexts (ship walls, army wings, mirror inversion) are not congruent, and the claim itself disclaims a formula. The survival of the old 'left' word in poetic or technical pairs is lexical, not phraseological.

πότνια = pátnī (*pótnih₂) and Ἠώς = uṣás- (*h₂éwsōs) are exact. HyAphr 223 and 230 (πότνια, Ἠώς) and RV 3.61.4b (uṣā́ḥ, pátnī) check. But the syntax differs: pátnī here governs a genitive (svásarasya), 'mistress of the homestead', whereas πότνια is a free honorific. Both are stock titles of many goddesses. The Greek pairing is not Homeric and occurs in just two lines of one hymn. Exact cognates with real generic risk.

ὄνομα = nā́man- = nąman- = nōmen and τίθημι = dhā- = Av. dā- = Lat. -dere (in-dere) are exact. Every anchor has the collocation with 'name' as direct object of *dʰeh₁-, mostly middle. Plato Theages 122d: ὄνομα, ἔθου, the father naming his son. RV 1.103.4d: nā́ma, dadhé, the son taking a name. AVŚ 5.1.6: dadhete, nāma. Also Sophist 225a and Phaedrus 267d. Supported by Od. 19.403-6, Vd 18.52 and Plautus nomen with indere. The choice of 'put' for naming, rather than 'call', recurs in at least four branches, with matching middle voice. Same verdict as B148.

Only *ph₂tḗr is cognate (pater = pitā). The theonym slot holds unrelated gods (Mars, Ianus vs Parjanya). The syntax differs: Cato 141.2 and 134.2-3 are vocative addresses (Mars or Iane with pater, then precor), while AVŚ 12.1.12 (DCS 12, 1.s26; parjanyaḥ, pitā) is a predicative statement paired with mātā, bhūmiḥ. 'Father' as a title for gods is universal. The Latin use of pater with any god is a Latin extension. The genuinely inherited part, the vocative *dyeu ph₂ter, is already covered by B113/B119. As a separate claim it is a single generic element.

λείχω = rih- (*leyǵʰ-) and ἀμβροσία ~ amṛ́ta- (*n̥-mr̥-tó-) are cognate. But the Vedic support is misconstrued. In RV 10.123.3d the subject of rihánti is vā́ṇīḥ (the voices), which lick the calf. mádhvaḥ, amŕ̥tasya are genitives depending on vā́ṇīḥ ('voices of the sweet immortal drink'), not the object of licking. The AV anchor 7.73.6 has amṛtāsaḥ as the immortal subjects licking the offering, not ambrosia as object. The only real witness is a comic line, Ar. Pax 854 (ἀμβροσίαν, λείχειν). The RV has 1 stanza with rih-, amŕ̥ta-, which is chance level.

āmá- = ὠμός, kravís- = κρέας and ad- = ἔδω are all exact cognates. AVŚ 8.6.48 really has āmaṃ, adanti and kraviḥ in one clause, of demons eating raw (human) flesh, and RV 1.162.10b has āmásya, kravíṣaḥ. Il. 22.347 has all three Greek reflexes in one line (ὤμ', κρέα, ἔδμεναι): Achilles' wish to devour Hector raw. Herodotus 3.99 (ἐδεσταί of raw κρεῶν, cannibals) also checks. The contexts agree: savage or demonic eating of human flesh. Vedic keeps the inherited *krewh₂- in this marked 'raw flesh' sense beside ordinary māṃsa-, and both sides build raw-eater agent nouns. The Hippocratic anchor is a mere dietary use, but the three-term match in congruent contexts is beyond chance (Homer has 1 line with ὠμός, κρέας).

Ἠώς = uṣás- is exact. devī́ (*deywih₂) and δῖα (fem. of δῖος = divyá-) share a root but are different formations, so the epithet is not an exact pair. The anchor is misread: in RV 10.127.3b, devī́ is Night (āyatī́, 'the coming goddess') and uṣásam is her sister, so they do not agree. Il. 18.255 (ἠῶ, δῖαν) is a stock Homeric formula. Real Vedic uṣā́ḥ, devī́ exists in support, but devī́ is applied to every goddess and δῖος to everything noble. One exact element plus a pair of generic epithets.

vṛka- = λύκος = вълкъ and avi- = ὄις = овьца are cognates (the Slavic is a derivative). But the images differ. AVP 1.72.4 is a gambler compared to a wolf that has seized a ewe. Hdt. 4.149 (ὄιν among λύκοισι) is 'a sheep among wolves'. Ar. Pax 1076 (λύκος with ὑμεναιοῖ) is an adynaton of a wolf marrying a sheep. The Primary Chronicle line is a proverb about a wolf raiding the flock. Wolf and sheep as predator and prey is the default image of every herding culture, built from default words. Not a shared collocation.

sumánas- = εὐμενής (*h₁su-menes-) is an exact compound. The anchors only partly fit a divine-favour formula. Plato Leges 927a uses εὐμενεῖς of the souls of the dead. AVŚ 3.4.11 (sumanasaḥ, bhavantu) is about wives and sons, and AVŚ 3.20.12 about the people. Only the AVŚ 3.20.3 context (agne ... sumanā, bhava) is a prayer to a god. The predicate 'be' is the default copula, and asking a deity to be well-disposed is universal. This is the inherited word used in its natural sense, not a distinct phrase. Same grade as B140.

The exact compound sumánas- = εὐμενής is used of gods whose favour is sought on both sides. Xen. Cyr. 2.1.1 and 3.3.21 (ἵλεως, εὐμενεῖς) and Hell. 6.4.2 (θεοὺς, εὐμενεστάτους) check, as do RV prayers with bháva, sumánāḥ (10 stanzas with sumánas-, bhū-). The context fits better than in B139. But the second element is the trivial copula or a different word (ἵλεως vs áheḷant-). The RV anchor 4.13.1b is descriptive, not a petition. A word meaning 'well-disposed' will naturally be used in prayers for divine goodwill. Lexical survival rather than a formula. Same grade as B139.

κλέος = śrávas-, μέγας = máh- and τίθημι = dhā- are cognate. RV 1.79.4c (dhehi with máhi śrávaḥ as object) and Hdt. 9.78.2 (κλέος as object of καταθέσθαι, with μέγιστον) check. The adjective-noun pair 'great fame' is strong: Homer has κλέος, μέγας in 13 lines (about 1.7 expected), and the RV has śrávas-, máh- in 25 stanzas (about 9 expected). But the verb element fails. Homer has no κλέος, τίθημι (1 line, Od. 2.125, where τιθεῖσι governs νόον). Greek κλέος, καταθέσθαι appears only in classical prose (Hdt. 7.220, 9.78; Plato Symp. 208c) and matches the ordinary prose idiom χάριν, καταθέσθαι 'lay up (as a deposit)' (Antiphon, Demosthenes). That is a Greek-internal metaphor, not a continuation of śrávo dhā-. RV 1.40.4b concerns ákṣiti, śrávaḥ, not 'great'. The three-term phrase is not shown to be inherited.

The Latvian anchor checks in the dainas book (BV 4989, Dieva, dēlu saddling a horse), and Hdt. 2.50.2 names the Διόσκουροι. Only the god element is related, and not as an exact form: Latv. Dievs < *deywós vs Gk Διός < *diwós. The 'son' word differs in every branch (dēls, κοῦρος, nápāt-). The mythological equation of horse-linked divine twins, sons of the sky god, is well founded, but as phraseology it is one element with renewal. The Herodotus anchor is just a list of god names. Defensible myth parallel, weak as wording.

The anchors check: Mirab. 114 has θέρος and χειμῶνος (fire in summer, icy water in winter), and AVŚ 13.1.96 has ghraṃsaḥ, himaḥ (heat and cold born from Rohita). χειμών/χεῖμα ~ himá- is cognate, but the heat word is not the same formation (θέρος vs ghraṃsá-/gharmá-; ghraṃsá- may be a separate root extension, so the anchor's heat word is not shown to be cognate with θέρος). The contexts are a paradoxography wonder and a cosmogonic list. A heat/cold or summer/winter polar pair in each language's default words is generic. Same verdict as B116.

sū́rya- = ἥλιος (*sóh₂wl̥) is exact. spáś- and σκοπός share *speḱ- (σκοπ- by the regular metathesis) but are different formations. The anchor RV 1.33.8d does not make the sun a watcher: Indra sets spies (spáśaḥ) around with the sun. The real Vedic witness is RV 4.13.3c-d (sū́ryam called spáśam of all that moves). With HH Dem. 62 (Ἠέλιον called σκοπόν of gods and men) it is a good match: the sun as watcher with a genitive of all beings. But the all-seeing sun is cross-cultural (e.g. Shamash), and the agent nouns are not identical.

*deh₃- 'give' and *h₁wésu- 'goods' are cognate: δίδωμι/δωτήρ = dā-/dātár- = Av. dā-/dātar-, and ἐύς (gen. pl. ἑάων) = vásu- = vohu-. The formula is solid in support: Od. 8.325 (gods as δωτῆρες, ἑάων) and 8.335 (δῶτορ, ἑάων) check; RV 8.51.5a (dātā́, vásūnām) checks; Y 65.12b (vohunąm, dātārō, of the Aməṣ̌a Spəṇtas) and Y 16.1b (dātārəm, vohunąm) check. The archaic ἑάων is confined to this formula. The anchors are partial. Il. 24.528 has δίδωσι with ἑάων (Zeus's jars), which is congruent. Y 39.4 dā̊s may be *dʰeh₁- rather than *deh₃- (Avestan merges them), and AVŚ 7.97.8 gives only vasūni. Accepted on the agent-noun formula, which is triple and exact.

Same equation as B127 (εὐρύς = urú-, πόντος = pánthā-), graded identically. The lead anchor Hdt. 2.116.3 quotes Il. 6.291 verbatim, so it is derivative of Homer and adds nothing independent. Hdt. 4.86.3 (εὐρύτατον predicated of the Pontus in a geographic measurement) is irrelevant. The Vedic anchors check. εὐρύς is a generic epithet of all Greek expanses (51 Homeric lines with sea, land or sky nouns), so the Greek half is explicable without inheritance.

aṃsa- = Umbr. onse = ὦμος and bhṛ- = fer- = φέρω are exact cognates. AVŚ 8.6.26 (aṃsa with bibhrati) and the Iguvine line with the words destre, onse, fertu (Buck text; the anchor's 'VIa 60' label looks like a line-number artefact of the OCR) check. But the contexts do not match: demons carrying their bodies vs a ritual instruction for carrying an implement. Carrying something on the shoulder is a universal action that any language describes with its ordinary 'shoulder' and 'carry' words. The claim concedes this.
checked_loci: Ig. VIa 60 (Buck OCR label; VIb 50 in the standard numbering)

reasons: Same inherited collocation as B133, graded identically: *h₁nómn̥ as object of middle *dʰeh₁-. Isaeus 3.30 (ὄνομα, θέσθαι, the father naming the child at the tenth-day feast) and Dem. 43.74 (ὀνόματα, ἐθέμην for his sons) check, both naming a child, as does RV 1.103.4d (nā́ma, dadhé). The voice differs slightly (reflexive vs indirect middle), but the choice of 'put' for naming recurs across Greek, Indo-Iranian and Latin (nomen with indere). The prose anchors are late but represent ordinary Greek usage continuous with Od. 19.406.
